The 5-day mean is the best of the three (+0.0203, t = 8.7, positive in all periods), though its gain over the 1-day version is only +0.0007 — under the 0.002 threshold. Two tests in a row have now failed to beat the best by a meaningful margin, so I'll stop and hand in the 5-day mean version.

What I found: the high–low range does carry information in the direction the idea states — coins whose daily range is wide go on to underperform — and the effect survives removal of the known styles (incremental IC +0.0203, t = 8.7). The single day was the best single-day reading (+0.0196), but averaging over 5 days kept the sign and the direction the idea asks for, with every period positive. The median version over 10 days was weaker (+0.0171) and the 10-day mean weaker still, so the signal lives in recent range expansion rather than in a long-run level.

The idea is about the daily gap: close above open means a positive gap. Since the raw gap is price-unit-independent, I'll start with the simplest version, the 5-day average of the daily gap, and see how much of it survives after reversal and momentum are removed.

rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw daily gap is fully absorbed by short-term reversal (it is essentially the same quantity as the daily return, which is already removed), so the plain 5-day average gives nothing incremental. The idea still says "far above open", so I'll keep the same direction but emphasize the extreme days by squaring the gap before averaging.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0156, 2023 -0.0099, 2024 -0.0056

Emphasizing extremes with squaring makes the signal real but points the wrong way: coins closing far above open underperform. I'll check whether that is an artifact of the 5-day window by measuring the same gap over a longer 10-day window instead.

The 10-day window is consistent with the 5-day one: the squared gap is real, and it is negative — coins closing far above open underperform, not continue. The only remaining question is whether the sign is just the reversal effect hiding a different component, so I'll measure the gap against the coin's own recent average gap (normalized, so it is comparable across coins and not a price-level level).

What I found: the gap between close and open is a real signal on this history, but it points the opposite way to the idea. Coins closing far above their open tend to underperform over the next days, with incremental IC −0.0103 at a t of −6.1, and the sign is stable in all three sub-periods (2022H2, 2023, 2024). Emphasizing the extremes (squaring) or stretching the window to 10 days did not change the sign, and the relative-gap version was weaker still, so the effect is not an artifact of one window. I keep the direction the idea states — the factor rises when the gap is large — and report honestly that the idea is wrong on this history.

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range: low within the range is bullish, high within the range is bearish. So the natural first form is a relative position: current quote volume ranked inside its own 20-day range, negated so that low positions score high.

error: sec_rank() has no argument 'window'

The rank operator itself doesn't take a window, so the 10-day version needs a range computed first and then the rank. I'll write it as a ratio of the last 10 days' volume to its own 60-day mean, negated.

A coin whose dollar volume sits low within its own recent range does bounce, and the effect survives after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — the 20-day version of the range gives incremental IC +0.0071 (t = 5.1) with the same sign in all three periods (2022H2 +0.0138, 2023 +0.0083, 2024 +0.0026). Shortening the band to 10 days or switching to medians both weakened it, so the signal is about the band being broad rather than narrow. The direction is as the idea states: low volume inside the band scores high.

The idea is about a recent surge in dollar volume: when dollar volume peaks, the coin falls back. So the quantity should be the current dollar volume relative to its own recent history — a ratio, so price units cancel. I'll start with the simplest version: 5-day mean dollar volume divided by its 20-day mean, negated because a high surge is bearish.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. The version with a 5-day mean dollar volume against a 20-day baseline gives incremental IC +0.0170 (t = 5.9) and is positive in all three periods (2022H2 +0.0220, 2023 +0.0199, 2024 +0.0116), which is what the idea predicts — a surge in dollar volume precedes underperformance. Shorter recent windows (3 days) are weaker, and the sign is reversed for coins whose dollar volume has just fallen to a new high. The effect is not just a repackaging of volatility or liquidity: it survives removal of those styles and is not a 5-day/20-day reversal signal.

So the effect is real but modest, and it lives at the 10-day level rather than in the extremes.

Since that position is bounded between 0 and 1, it is comparable across coins regardless of price unit, and the direction is negative.
